words.intro: Heidelberg has a ruined castle, a very old bridge, and one long main street. It is impossible to get lost here, and tourists manage it daily.

opener.caption: Heidelberg, von der Alten Brücke aus. Da oben ist das Schloss.
reading.intro: Maya is in Heidelberg for the day and wants to see the old bridge. An elderly man on the market square is delighted to be asked. He has lived here all his life, and he knows every street.
reading.photos[0].caption: Das Brückentor: Hier gehen seit Jahrhunderten alle durch.
reading.photos[1].caption: Auf der Alten Brücke: Fünfzig Meter. Maya hat sie gefunden.
reading.en: Maya: Excuse me, how do I get to the Old Bridge? · Mann: To the bridge? That’s very easy. Where are you from? · Maya: From Berlin. I’ve come from the station. · Mann: Right. First go straight on to the church. At the church turn left, into the little street. Then up the stairs to the castle. · Maya: To the castle? But I want to go to the bridge. · Mann: Yes, yes. You can see everything from the castle! Then go through the garden, past the university, and then keep right. You can’t miss it. · An hour later. Maya has walked four thousand steps. She’s tired. She comes round the corner and is back on the market square. There sits the man. · Maya: You! I’m back here! So where is the bridge? · Mann: The bridge? There. · He points with his finger. Behind the café, fifty metres away, stands the Old Bridge. · Maya: Fifty metres! Why didn’t you tell me? · Mann: Otherwise you’d have seen nothing. The castle was nice, wasn’t it? A coffee?
reading.fact: Heidelberg’s castle has been a ruin since the French blew it up in the 1690s, and Germans have liked it better that way ever since. Mark Twain wrote about it, and its cellar holds one of the largest wine barrels in the world.
document.caption: Ein Wegweiser: Wie weit ist es?
document.intro: A real signpost in St. Wendel, a town in Saarland. Every German old town has one for walkers. The brown signs are for sights, the white for the things you need, and the number is how many metres it is. All of these point left.
document.fact: *Wandern* is taken seriously here: the forest paths are marked with small painted symbols, and clubs repaint them by hand. In Germany there are more than 200,000 km of marked trails, nearly all of it looked after by volunteers.
